## CLINICAL RECOMMENDATION

Based on Cochrane-level evidence, single-visit and multiple-visit root canal treatment of necrotic teeth with apical periodontitis produce equivalent long-term outcomes for radiographic healing, tooth retention, swelling, flare-up, and analgesic use, so either regimen is clinically acceptable [[PMID:36512807]]. Clinicians should note the one consistent trade-off: single-visit treatment carries a modestly higher risk of pain within the first postoperative week (moderate-certainty evidence) [[PMID:36512807]]. Case selection should therefore be driven by ability to achieve adequate disinfection and a well-sealed coronal restoration at the same visit — factors that are independently more predictive of success than visit number [[PMID:38243912]]. When bacterial elimination is uncertain at the first visit (e.g., large lesions, persistent exudate, complex anatomy), a multiple-visit protocol with calcium hydroxide dressing remains a reasonable, historically supported option [[PMID:9477818]].

---

## EVIDENCE SUMMARY

**Cochrane Reviews**

The Mergoni et al. 2022 Cochrane review is the most authoritative synthesis, including 47 RCTs and 5693 teeth analysed [[PMID:36512807]]. It found no evidence of a difference between single- and multiple-visit treatment for tooth extraction (very low certainty), radiological failure (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.81–1.07; moderate certainty, 13 studies), swelling/flare-up, analgesic use, or sinus tract presence [[PMID:36512807]]. The one clinically meaningful difference was a higher proportion of participants reporting pain within one week in single-visit groups (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.14–2.09; moderate certainty), an effect that was more pronounced in vital teeth and when mechanical instrumentation was used [[PMID:36512807]]. This finding has been consistent across the 2007, 2016, and 2022 iterations of the review, indicating stability of the conclusion.

**Level I — RCTs and Systematic Reviews**

Position statements support this equipoise. The ESE 2023 Quality Guidelines state that single-visit root canal treatment is appropriate for most cases, while endorsing calcium silicate sealers and bioceramic materials that facilitate efficient single-visit workflows (ESE-QG-2023). ESE outcome data indicate healing rates of 68–85% at 4 years for teeth with pre-operative apical periodontitis, driven primarily by preparation and obturation quality rather than by number of visits (ESE-PS-VPT-2019). Recent RCTs in aging populations reinforce comparable outcomes: Dong et al. reported 1-year success rates of 91–95% across single-cone, warm vertical compaction, and cold lateral condensation techniques, with no significant difference in PAI reduction [[PMID:40375218]]. Alzoubi et al. found 12-month success rates of 76.6–80.5% (PAI) whether sealer-based obturation or warm vertical compaction was employed in a single-visit protocol [[PMID:40653155]].

**Level II — Prospective Studies**

Almeida et al. designed a three-arm RCT comparing single-visit, two-visit with calcium hydroxide dressing, and two-visit without dressing in molars with asymptomatic apical periodontitis, with CBCT-assessed periradicular repair at 24 months as the primary endpoint — a study specifically addressing whether intracanal medication adds value when ultrasonic irrigant activation is used [[PMID:36635764]]. Results have not yet been published, but the design reflects the current uncertainty about whether enhanced single-visit disinfection eliminates any residual advantage of multiple visits. Simon et al.'s multicentre RCT with bioceramic sealers (n=160) reported 24-month success rates of 86.6–87.7% across primary and secondary treatments — consistent with the ceiling suggested by systematic reviews and independent of visit number [[PMID:40491343]].

**Level IIIa — Retrospective Cohort Studies**

Jurič et al.'s 13-year cohort (n=1259 teeth, 91% recall) identified single-visit treatment as an independent negative prognostic factor at the tooth level (OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.21–0.75 vs multiple visits), alongside unsatisfactory root filling quality, filling not ending within 2 mm of the apex, resin sealer (vs bioceramic), and defective coronal restoration [[PMID:38243912]]. This finding sits in apparent tension with the Cochrane pooled estimate but is consistent with real-world case-mix effects: single-visit decisions in complex cases may reflect selection bias, and the effect of visit number was smaller than the effects of obturation quality, coronal seal, and preoperative lesion severity [[PMID:38243912]]. Vieira et al. similarly identified higher number of treatment visits without intracanal medication as a negative outcome factor, whereas overextension, presence of preoperative lesion, and lesion size >10 mm were the dominant prognostic variables [[PMID:38214429]].

**Classic / Foundational**

Sjögren et al.'s foundational microbiological work established that when post-instrumentation cultures are positive, 5-year success falls to 68% versus 94% for culture-negative cases in single-appointment obturation of teeth with apical periodontitis [[PMID:9477818]]. The authors concluded that reliable eradication of infection in a single visit is not consistently achievable without an interappointment antimicrobial dressing [[PMID:9477818]]. Sjögren et al.'s earlier 8–10 year outcome study similarly showed that success in necrotic teeth with periapical radiolucency (86%) was substantially lower than in cases without radiolucency (>96%), underscoring the primacy of preoperative status over procedural details [[PMID:2084204]]. These classic studies predate modern rotary instrumentation, ultrasonic activation, and bioceramic sealers, and their applicability to contemporary single-visit protocols is limited — but they remain the mechanistic rationale for multiple-visit treatment when adequate disinfection is uncertain.

## CLINICAL RECOMMENDATION

Based on Cochrane-level evidence, single-visit and multiple-visit root canal treatment yield equivalent long-term outcomes for necrotic teeth with apical periodontitis, with no meaningful difference in radiographic healing, tooth extraction, swelling/flare-up, or sinus tract resolution [[PMID:36512807]]. Choice of protocol should therefore be driven by case-specific factors (case complexity, ability to achieve dryness and disinfection, patient tolerance), while the clinician counsels that single-visit treatment carries a modestly higher risk of transient post-obturation pain within the first week [[PMID:36512807]]. Where infection persists — particularly a positive culture immediately before obturation — a multi-visit approach with an interappointment calcium hydroxide dressing remains a defensible option supported by classic prognostic evidence [[PMID:9477818]].

---

## EVIDENCE SUMMARY

**Cochrane Reviews**

The most recent Cochrane review (Mergoni et al. 2022) synthesised 47 RCTs comprising 5,693 teeth and found no evidence of a difference between single-visit and multiple-visit root canal treatment for the primary outcomes of tooth extraction (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.09–2.50; very low certainty) or radiological failure at ≥1 year (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.81–1.07; moderate certainty) [[PMID:36512807]]. There was no difference in swelling/flare-up, analgesic use, or sinus tract presence. The one signal favouring multi-visit protocols was a higher proportion of patients reporting pain within the first week after single-visit treatment (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.14–2.09; moderate certainty), an effect that was most pronounced in vital teeth and when mechanical instrumentation was used [[PMID:36512807]]. Notably, this review specifically excluded older trials that did not use rubber dam isolation and sodium hypochlorite irrigation, strengthening the applicability of its findings to contemporary practice.

**Level I — RCTs and Systematic Reviews**

Position statements from the ESE support single-visit root canal treatment as appropriate for most cases when adequate disinfection can be achieved, aligning with the Cochrane conclusion [[PMID:ESE-QG-2023]]. A large RCT of 240 older patients treated in a single visit with bioceramic or resin sealer obturation reported 1-year success rates of 91–95% across all groups, demonstrating that single-visit protocols perform well in modern clinical practice when case selection is appropriate [[PMID:40375218]]. An ongoing three-arm RCT by Almeida et al. is specifically comparing single-visit, two-visit with calcium hydroxide, and two-visit without medication protocols in mandibular molars with apical periodontitis using ultrasonic irrigant activation and CBCT-verified healing at 24 months — results will help clarify whether ultrasonic-enhanced disinfection makes intracanal medication redundant [[PMID:36635764]].

**Level IIIa — Retrospective Cohort Studies**

The largest recent cohort (Jurič et al., n=1,259 teeth followed 1–4 years) identified single-visit treatment as an independent negative prognostic factor at the tooth level (OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.21–0.75) when compared against multiple-visit treatment, alongside preoperative apical periodontitis severity, technical quality of the root filling, and coronal restoration quality [[PMID:38243912]]. This finding contrasts with the Cochrane synthesis of RCTs, and the discrepancy likely reflects case-mix confounding in real-world practice — single-visit treatment may have been selected preferentially for less complex cases, or conversely, higher-risk cases without capacity for interappointment disinfection. Vieira et al. (n=304) similarly found a higher number of treatment visits without intracanal medication negatively affected outcome, indirectly supporting the value of interappointment disinfection when multiple visits are used [[PMID:38214429]].

**Classic / Foundational**

Sjögren et al.'s seminal single-visit trial of 55 single-rooted teeth with apical periodontitis showed that periapical healing occurred in 94% of teeth with a negative culture at the time of obturation but only 68% when the pre-obturation culture was positive — a statistically significant difference emphasising that residual infection at the time of filling predicts failure [[PMID:9477818]]. The authors argued that reliable eradication of bacteria could not be achieved in a single visit without interappointment medication. This is the historical basis for the multi-visit approach, though contemporary irrigation protocols (higher NaOCl concentrations, ultrasonic activation) may narrow this gap and are the reason older trials were excluded from the current Cochrane review [[PMID:36512807]]. Sjögren et al.'s long-term outcomes study of 356 patients similarly established preoperative pulp/periapical status as the dominant determinant of outcome, with success falling to 86% in teeth with necrosis and periapical radiolucency [[PMID:2084204]].

## CLINICAL RECOMMENDATION

Based on Cochrane-level evidence, single-visit and multiple-visit root canal treatment yield equivalent long-term outcomes for necrotic teeth with apical periodontitis, with no significant difference in radiographic healing, tooth extraction, swelling, flare-up, or sinus tract at ≥12 months [[PMID:36512807]]. The choice between protocols should therefore be driven by case-specific factors (canal disinfection achieved, patient tolerance, restorability, scheduling) rather than a categorical preference. Clinicians should counsel patients that single-visit treatment carries a modestly higher risk of postoperative pain within the first week (moderate-certainty evidence) [[PMID:36512807]], and that adequate chemomechanical disinfection and a well-sealed coronal restoration remain the strongest predictors of success regardless of visit number [[PMID:38243912]].

---

## EVIDENCE SUMMARY

**Cochrane Reviews**

The 2022 Cochrane review by Mergoni et al. is the definitive synthesis on this question, incorporating 47 RCTs with 5,805 participants and 5,693 teeth [[PMID:36512807]]. Moderate-certainty evidence showed no difference in radiological failure between single-visit and multiple-visit protocols (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.81–1.07; 13 studies, 1,505 teeth), and no difference in tooth extraction, swelling/flare-up, analgesic use, or sinus tract presence. However, the review found moderate-certainty evidence that single-visit treatment increases the proportion of patients reporting pain within one week (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.14–2.09), with the effect most pronounced in vital teeth and when mechanical instrumentation was used. Notably, subgroup data specifically on necrotic teeth did not show a divergent healing pattern, supporting the conclusion that neither approach is superior for the necrotic/apical periodontitis presentation. The authors emphasise that neither regimen prevents post-treatment complications in the 12-month window.

**Level I — RCTs and Systematic Reviews**

The ESE 2023 quality guidelines endorse single-visit root canal treatment as appropriate for most cases, consistent with the Cochrane synthesis, provided disinfection standards are met (ESE Position Statement 2023). The ESE outcome statement notes healing rates of 68–85% for teeth with pre-operative apical periodontitis at 4 years, with preparation and obturation quality — not visit number — being the strongest predictors of success (ESE Position Statement 2019). Almeida et al. published a protocol for an ongoing three-arm RCT (single-visit vs. two-visit with Ca(OH)₂ vs. two-visit without medication) in mandibular molars with apical periodontitis, using CBCT assessment at 24 months, which will further refine this question [[PMID:36635764]]. Ahmad's 2025 RCT in 302 necrotic molars with symptomatic apical periodontitis treated in a single visit demonstrated that adjunctive intracanal cryotherapy significantly reduces postoperative pain at 6, 24 and 72 hours — a relevant mitigation strategy given the Cochrane finding of higher early pain with single-visit protocols [[PMID:40297278]].

**Classic / Foundational**

Sjögren et al. (1997) provided the mechanistic foundation for concerns about single-visit treatment of infected canals: in 55 single-rooted teeth with apical periodontitis treated in one visit, healing occurred in 94% of cases with negative pre-obturation cultures versus only 68% when positive cultures remained — a significant difference — leading the authors to argue that inter-appointment antimicrobial dressing is needed to reliably eradicate infection [[PMID:9477818]]. Sjögren et al. (1990) similarly showed that necrotic teeth with periapical radiolucency had lower healing rates (86%) than vital cases (>96%) at 8–10 years, underscoring the disinfection challenge in this specific presentation [[PMID:2084204]]. These foundational findings drove decades of two-visit advocacy; however, the aggregate RCT evidence synthesised by Cochrane has not confirmed a clinically detectable healing advantage for multi-visit protocols when contemporary chemomechanical preparation with NaOCl irrigation is used [[PMID:36512807]].

**Level IIIa — Retrospective Cohort**

Jurič et al.'s 13-year single-endodontist cohort of 1,259 teeth (recall rate 91%) identified single-visit treatment as an independent factor associated with reduced odds of success (OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.21–0.75) alongside suboptimal root filling quality, resin (vs. bioceramic) sealer, and defective coronal restoration [[PMID:38243912]]. This finding partially contradicts the Cochrane conclusion, but the study's observational design, single-operator context, and inability to fully adjust for case-mix (single-visit cases may have been selected for less complex presentations, or vice versa) limit its ability to override Level I evidence. Vieira et al.'s retrospective analysis of 304 treatments found that a higher number of treatment visits without intracanal medication negatively affected outcome — supporting the position that when multiple visits are used, appropriate interappointment medication matters [[PMID:38214429]]. Both cohorts reinforce that visit number is subordinate to technical execution and coronal seal.
